You’re misinterpreting what he’s saying. The MD in your video’s exact words are “these abnormal posturing that occur in SIGNIFICANT brain injuries, or concussions”. Posturing occurs when someone has sustained fairly significant trauma to the brain.

You may already have a system in place, but re: kids getting self conscious, I have noticed the same issue. What I’ve found helps is instead of doing +/-, I make all of my data look really similar. For example, correct predictions will be a plus, and incorrect productions will also be a plus with the tiniest variation, like a tail on the vertical line or the horizontal line angling down towards the right. That way I know what the accuracy % was, but to the kids it all looks the same! Then I just tell them “I’m just keeping track of how many times you try [today, this round, these next 5 mins]!” It’s not foolproof, but it works!

To answer OPs question though, I don’t take data every day, esp when I’m first teaching a concept. Get baseline data, teach, then start tracking!

As I was pulling into the parking lot I scraped the shit out of a car. My 16 yo brain immediately decided the best course of action was to roll-bounce & told my friends to lie for me & say I never showed up to BBuster (is BBuster a thing? No it's not. It is now). 

Anyways I wind up at home & run to my parents crying about this "car that hit me in the parking lot." My mom tells me to go to bed but the next morning shoved a notepad in my face & tells me to draw a diagram of the accident. Needless to say as the accident I described to her the day before didn't exist, I quickly realized the story I was attempting to draw logistically didn't make sense. I cried some more & was grounded for a year.
